blocks.text: The chapter moves through Mary Magdalene’s encounter and commission, Jesus’ appearances to the gathered disciples, and Thomas’s confession. Testimony, recognition, Jesus’ wounded body, peace, the gift of the Spirit, and belief are held together across these scenes; the closing verses then explain that the written signs are selected to lead to belief and life.

Although this book is traditionally called John, the continuous Greek Gospel does not name its narrator or give the author’s personal name in its purpose statement. The chapter’s reference to “the disciple whom Jesus loved” therefore does not itself identify that figure as John son of Zebedee.

Several questions in this chapter remain debated. John 20:23 closely joins Jesus’ sending of the disciples, the Spirit, and the forgiving or retaining of sins. Readers have understood this in ecclesial, communal, declarative, disciplinary, and sacramental ways; none of those readings permits coercion or concealing crime.

The purpose statement in verses 30–31 appears before John 21, which functions as an epilogue. Whether that later chapter was composed later or by another hand is disputed. Manuscripts also differ between wording often translated “may believe” and “may continue believing”; that difference alone does not securely settle whether the statement addresses new believers or existing ones. Proposals that the Gospel was assembled from sources or editions likewise remain unconfirmed, since no proposed source or edition survives independently.
